paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: All languages change. English speakers today would struggle to read the English of Chaucer, written about 1390, and would find Old English, the language of Beowulf, as foreign as German. Yet no speaker ever decided to change the language, and few notice it happening in their own lifetimes. The mechanisms of linguistic change have fascinated scholars for centuries, and modern research has made them better understood, though not entirely predictable.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Change begins in the speech of individuals. A new pronunciation, word or grammatical form appears, usually among younger speakers or a particular social group, and may spread if others imitate it. Whether it does depends partly on prestige: forms associated with admired groups spread more readily. Sociolinguists such as William Labov showed in studies of New York speech that changes often start in the middle of the social scale and are pushed upwards by people seeking to sound more successful.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Sound change is the most systematic type. Over generations, sounds tend to shift in regular patterns. The Great Vowel Shift, which took place in English between about 1400 and 1700, changed the pronunciation of long vowels, so that the word house, once pronounced roughly like hoose, acquired its modern sound. Because the shift affected all words with the same vowel, while spelling had become fixed, written English now preserves traces of an older pronunciation, which is why English spelling seems so inconsistent.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Vocabulary changes faster, driven by technology, contact and fashion. Languages borrow from each other: English has taken words from more than a hundred languages, including algebra from Arabic and kindergarten from German. Meanings also drift. Nice once meant foolish, and awful meant inspiring awe. Speakers often regard such changes as decay, but linguists see them as natural: no variety is more correct than another, only more or less accepted in a given setting.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Can change be controlled? Some countries have language academies, such as the Académie française, which publish recommendations for correct usage. Their influence is limited. Despite efforts to replace English borrowings with French equivalents, many French speakers continue to say le weekend. In the long run, a language belongs to those who use it, and it will change as long as there are people who speak it. A language that stops changing is, in practice, a dead one.
